1.title: Good-bye to home; a crowded first night
highlights: After bidding everyone good-bye, the family waits beside the road while Clarence goes into Grinnell. A fire inside their traveling house keeps them comfortable in the cold.
At Ladora they leave the tent packed and all bunk together. The free campground is so close to the railroad that their first night on the road brings little rest.

2.title: A forgotten tent and two very different welcomes
highlights: Crossing the Mississippi brings the children's first glimpse of an elevated railroad and the family's first taste of city traffic.
In Rock Island they discover the tent is still on the Iowa side, where they removed it to inspect an oil leak. Back they go. Miriam jokes about a black cat and superstition.
With the engine missing and rain threatening, one farmhouse refuses them a camping place; the next welcomes them. They put up the recovered tent, pop corn, and finally get a good night's sleep.

3.title: Roadside kindness, a rolling kitchen, and a missing dog
highlights: Their hosts send them away with pears and onions. On a smooth stretch of Illinois road, Miriam peels potatoes, lights the heater, and starts dinner while Clarence drives.
At the dinner stop they discover they have left Jimmie behind. Miriam makes a rueful joke about every dog having his day; this entry does not describe recovering him.
By evening, news of a broken levee and flooding at Beardstown stops their plans. Clarence and Grover go into town to find out whether they can cross.

4.title: The flood sends them the long way around
highlights: Grover, Clarence, Mildred, and Kenneth walk three miles toward the ferry to investigate. The river is wild, Beardstown is flooded, and the crossing is impossible.
They turn back toward Quincy. Miriam accepts that it will be the long way around, but keeps collecting the day's surprises.
A sign at Camp Point offers a memorable warning: go slowly to see the city, or go fast and see the jail.

4.title: First riverboats; a tight squeeze into Missouri
highlights: Bridge detours near Quincy are so narrow that one nearly tears off the camper's side curtain.
Crossing the Mississippi gives the children their first sight of a steamer, towboat, and barges. Miriam calls the river a wonderful sight.
Missouri immediately feels rougher and steeper. They reach camp at Palmyra, where another traveling party has come from Louisiana.

5.title: Chocolate fudge for a sour repair crew
highlights: Sharp Missouri stones and slipping tires keep stopping the Ford. As Clarence and Grover grow disgusted, Miriam makes chocolate fudge to sweeten their tempers.
A construction stretch throws things out of the cupboard and cabinet. Nothing breaks, but everyone must stop to put the house back in order.
Miriam pauses amid the frustration to reflect that leaving home reveals how big the world is, and how little of it they have seen.

5.title: The little old Ford rambles on
highlights: A pothole breaks the strap holding the spare tires. Then the engine refuses to go; pushing does not help until they find trouble with the timer.
Another tire goes down before evening. Miriam counts three tire failures that day, with hills and unexpected curves between them.
Darkness catches them as they reach Louisiana, Missouri. Even finding the campground becomes a challenge after a day when every mile has felt hard-earned.

6.title: Small discoveries during another day of stops
highlights: At their campsite, nursery workers gather for a large six-wheel bus. More company buses follow, including separate buses for women.
The Mississippi bluffs and a crystal-clear creek over flat white rock give Miriam something lovely to record between repairs.
While another tire is being changed, the children entertain themselves with Missouri stones and someone's chicken coop as a target.

6.title: Pavement at last; then another blowout
highlights: The Ford stalls on a steep grade when low gear will not take hold. They block the wheels, tighten the low band, push, and climb on.
Everyone celebrates reaching pavement. Twenty minutes later, a blowout ends the celebration; Miriam says she now understands calling Missouri 'misery.'
At St. Charles they put up the tent, make supper, and pop corn. Somehow the day's troubles become something to laugh about together.

7.title: Into St. Louis, dirt and all
highlights: The approach to St. Louis is crowded with cars, signs, filling stations, and eating houses. Even Sunday traffic makes a strong impression.
They park at Sun Down campground while Clarence and Grover look for their hosts. The children try to occupy themselves during the wait.
Jack and Mr. Carnes arrive with a honk. Everyone climbs into their car, travel dirt and all, and heads into the city for a welcome afternoon of visiting.

8.title: A good sleep and the work of catching up
highlights: After enjoying a proper night's rest, the family returns to the camper to collect its dirty clothes. Miriam's day in the city includes washing them.
Clarence, Jack, and Grover combine sightseeing with a search for suitable tires.
Miriam looks forward to the women's turn at sightseeing tomorrow: even a city visit has to fit around the traveling household's needs.

9.title: A postponed outing becomes a day of visiting
highlights: The tire search is still unsuccessful, so the planned sightseeing trip must wait another day.
Miriam and Essie explore the nearby suburban shopping streets, where stores seem to lie in every direction.
They visit until midnight. After a week of difficult travel, simply having time together becomes part of the trip.

10.title: Moving stairs and a city like an ant hill
highlights: Four floors of ten-cent goods at Woolworth's astonish Miriam: where do so many different things come from?
At a department store she and Clarence ride an escalator for the first time. She carefully explains how to step on, stand still, and step off without losing balance.
They pay extra to reach the Railway Exchange building's roof. Holding their hats against the wind, they watch traffic below shrink to miniature toys in a busy ant hill.

10.title: An afternoon made for the children
highlights: Mr. Carnes takes the family to Forest Park. The children especially enjoy the bears, whose hillside dens, rocks, and running water impress Miriam.
The bird house and beautiful park drives make the afternoon as memorable as the morning's city heights.
The day ends with more visiting at the Kesters' home and another late bedtime: a full day of pleasures rather than roadside repairs.

11.title: A household's curiosity on a city's scale
highlights: At Chain of Rocks, the family looks across the meeting of the Missouri and Mississippi rivers before touring the waterworks.
Miriam is fascinated by the enormous working pumps and by the sequence of tanks that turns muddy river water into a city's supply.
Watching workers remove deep deposits of mud makes the work real to her. The family leaves feeling it has had a wonderful time and learned a great deal.

11.title: The city after dark has another side
highlights: On the return trip, Miriam notices gas lamps still being lit by hand. Heavy after-work traffic makes her glad to reach home safely.
The evening brings grim news: a streetcar motorman staying in the building has struck a woman, whose injuries are reported as likely fatal.
Jack is also badly bruised while helping move a wrecked automobile. His leg is caught between the car and a waterplug; Miriam says it is nearly broken.

12.title: One last evening before the road
highlights: Clarence and Jack visit the auto club to get a route out of St. Louis. With the tires changed and the Ford brought back from camp, they are ready to travel again.
Miriam looks back warmly on the visit. The men spend the evening at a bowling alley while the women turn in.
Rain falls through much of the night before their planned departure.

13.title: Autumn color and curiosity in the Ozarks
highlights: Leaving Essie and the children in the rain is followed by a magnificent drive through autumn woods. Miriam wishes everyone at home could see the colors.
Huge gray mounds near Bonne Terre puzzle the travelers. They stop to ask and learn that they are waste from lead mines.
Curiosity turns the journey into a roadside lesson: Miriam contrasts the gray lead waste with the red ground and water around iron mines.

13.title: A schoolyard becomes their bedroom
highlights: Rough dirt roads shake the bottom of the cupboard loose, nearly spilling their preserved fruit.
They fail to reach a town before dark and camp in a schoolyard, with water running across a low part of the nearby road.
Inside the one-room school, the children find long benches, bare windows, a wood heater, and a pile of fuel. They decide they would not care to attend school there.

14.title: A whole day lost to the tire search
highlights: Only a few miles into the morning, another tire fails on roads Miriam calls the worst yet.
Local inquiries produce nothing useful. Grover takes a bus thirty miles back to Flat River to look for replacements.
He does not return until eleven at night, and comes back without tires. Even a bright, sunny day cannot get them moving again.

15.title: New truck tires, new hope
highlights: The search finally succeeds: new wheels, tubes, and proper truck tires arrive. Miriam hopes this will end their tire troubles.
Changing the wheels occupies much of the day. Meanwhile, the household does its work and rearranges the little traveling home.
A late start leaves them climbing long, winding grades until darkness forces another filling-station camp.

16.title: Two cold visitors at the camper door
highlights: Before breakfast, two young men knock. They have slept in a car, one without a coat, and are nearly frozen. Miriam lets them warm up before they continue toward St. Louis.
Later the Ford stops again. A broken switch wire is found and repaired before they can continue.
The family's first cotton fields prompt a stop to gather a little to send home. Miriam also notices how exhausting the picking looks, rather than seeing only the crop.

17.title: Strangers become company
highlights: While the family works on its own Ford, two women traveling from Chicago to Florida stop to ask where they can find a garage.
Grover discovers that their broken dashboard makes steering dangerous. He gets a replacement board and repairs it for them.
The repair brings Miriam four or five hours of company while she does the washing. Their enforced stop becomes a chance to help fellow travelers.

18.title: Doll clothes and concern for the neighbors
highlights: A stationary day leaves time to write letters and help the children make doll clothes.
The rebuilt engine will not start, so departure must wait again.
An elderly couple arrives with an old horse and worn wagon, looking miserably cold. Miriam shares coffee and hopes tomorrow's sun will shine for their sake as well as her own.

19.title: A small gift before moving on
highlights: The Ford finally starts after a paid tow. Before leaving, the family gives the cold elderly travelers its remaining wood and a dollar.
Miriam wonders whether one good turn may bring another. Compassion, not just repairs, marks the end of their long stop.
At Osceola they camp opposite a carnival and all go over after supper. The music, whistles, and engines make it the noisiest town Miriam has encountered.

20.title: Turning west; a camp in name only
highlights: They finally leave the highway that has carried them so far south and turn west through Arkansas.
Pavement gives way to narrow, dusty gravel roads, with timber and sawmill logs along the way.
At Widener, a great sign promises a tourist camp. What they find looks more like a junkyard: bare ground and a large shed. They stay anyway.

21.title: An unfamiliar landscape becomes a puzzle
highlights: With sweaters off and curtains raised, the day feels like September in Iowa. A great blue heron rises from the swamp beside the road.
Strange derricks and wet fields puzzle the family. They stop for a sample, then learn at Carlisle that the crop is rice and the derricks are pumps.
Miriam begins to recognize the irrigation ditches once she understands what she is seeing: the drive keeps changing what looks familiar.

22.title: Hot Springs water steams like a teakettle
highlights: Little Rock offers a fine view of the capitol and its river bridges. Beyond the city, Miriam collects the fanciful names on homes, including Dew Drops and Lonesome Pine.
At Hot Springs, grand hotels and bathhouses line the route. Drinking fountains give off steam like water from a teakettle.
Miriam notes the many people seeking treatment there. The attraction is not simply a pretty city, but a place shaped around its remarkable hot water.

22.title: Their first real mountain roads
highlights: The hills become high enough to demand a brake adjustment. While the men work, the others gather hickory nuts.
Narrow roads through rock and tall trees feel like a new level of mountain travel. A long climb makes the Ford boil.
A clay hole sends the camper nearly sideways and frightens everyone. By evening they settle at a Ford station as drizzle returns.

23.title: Kenneth's long-feared ferry crossing
highlights: Miriam jokes that they never pass other cars; they let the other cars pass them. Roadside cattle and winding timber roads make patient driving necessary.
At the Red River, a ferry powered by a Fordson tractor carries their rig, another truck, and four touring cars.
Kenneth has worried about this crossing ever since learning there would be a ferry. They make it across, then continue through Texarkana into Texas.

24.title: Texas is not the warmth they expected
highlights: Ice forms in the washbasin overnight. The family had imagined Texas would be warm; instead, this is their coldest night so far.
Losing the route in Paris gives them an unintended look around a city Miriam admires.
Beyond town, broad prairie opens ahead and the paved road is visible for miles. At camp near Commerce, they register and buy milk and butter from the keeper.

25.title: Dallas joins the family
highlights: Near Dallas, the men stop to collect wood. Kenneth discovers a little rat terrier puppy in a gunny sack.
The family names the puppy Dallas. Miriam's verdict is simple: all the children are happy now.
The day's other roadside characters include covered-wagon travelers, rope reins, great mustaches, and the Texas hats the family knows from pictures.

25.title: Lost in two cities; airplanes at camp
highlights: Poor route markings make Dallas difficult to escape. Fort Worth is no easier: one set of directions assumes local knowledge, and even a policeman cannot identify their highway.
Another filling-station inquiry finally gets them out. A nail in a tire adds one more delay.
Their prairie campground has an aviation field nearby. After a trying day, the children have a new delight: watching airplanes land.

26.title: Texas is not all prairie
highlights: Street names are staked across open prairie near the growing cities. Miriam imagines these empty stretches as future neighborhoods.
Beyond Mineral Wells, twisting climbs and rocky drops overturn the family's picture of Texas as flat country.
An overheated engine gives them a stop for photographs of the children. Near Ranger, the view changes again: oil derricks and a great refinery fill the landscape.

27.title: A house nearly twisted in two
highlights: Oil wells remain visible in every direction as they leave Eastland.
A rough detour toward Abilene and more bridge detours afterward punish the camper. Miriam says one nearly twists their house in two.
Strong wind adds to the effort of driving. The day's real story is the strain of keeping a fragile moving household together over unfinished roads.

28.title: Spring birds and sermons on the rocks
highlights: Warmth, green growth, and early birdsong make November feel like spring. The children laugh at chicken nests made from kegs up in trees.
Religious messages appear high on projecting rocks. Miriam wonders how anyone could stand on those narrow ledges long enough to paint them.
Sand burrs provide a less welcome discovery: they stick, sting, and make a person dance.

28.title: Imagining earlier travelers across the prairie
highlights: Long stretches offer no water or shade, only low growth and an immense view. Miriam imagines what crossing toward California during the gold rush must have been like.
She notices concrete dips that carry water across the road instead of familiar Iowa culverts.
After rejecting one camp in Midland, they find a free campground outside town. Other traveling parties share the chilly, windy night.

29.title: Long empty miles and other motorists' remains
highlights: Quail provide dinner, and a lone goat and a coyote become notable sights in an otherwise nearly empty landscape.
A detour winds through sagebrush on a stony road lined with discarded tires and tubes. Miriam pities anyone attempting it on four poor tires.
Sand mounds and long gaps between settlements make the distance palpable. Straight pavement can stretch out of sight both ahead and behind.

30.title: Wildlife between the mountain ranges
highlights: A pond with wild ducks appears unexpectedly among the barren hills. Grover shoots two for supper.
The family gets its first look at prairie dogs. Miriam describes kitten-sized animals that sit like squirrels and bark like puppies.
Mountain distances are deceptive: a range that seems close takes miles to reach. A one-way railway underpass warns drivers that they may meet a fool.

30.title: Wind, dust, and an expensive stopping place
highlights: Round clumps of weeds blow down the road like rolling wheels. Dust grows so thick that the driver must slow because he cannot see ahead.
Dirty and dusty, the family decides to stop at Sierra Blanca rather than press on.
The prices of milk and butter strike them as a hold-up, so they buy neither. Still, the campground is company: seven other parties are there.

31.title: Learning to read the Rio Grande valley
highlights: Adobe houses fascinate Miriam. She records their flat roofs, drainage spouts, and mud bricks drying before construction.
Horses grazing loose in the fields puzzle the family until Kenneth sees a picker load a sack onto one and ride it to the wagon.
Shade trees and settled valley towns make a startling contrast with the empty stretches behind them. Miriam thinks this part of Texas could look like a garden of Eden.

31.title: Six letters make everyone happy
highlights: At El Paso, the family receives six letters. Miriam says a person cannot know how good mail feels until being away from it for so long.
The campground offers showers, laundry, and a cookhouse, though their own outfit supplies what they need. Miriam does her washing during the stop.
At half past eleven, everyone else is asleep. She addresses her diary as the little old book keeping her company, then says good night.

32.title: Good-bye, Texas; an unexpected inspection
highlights: Grover recognizes a man from an earlier journey. The family also celebrates getting through El Paso without losing the route for once.
Near their Rio Grande crossing, the river has dwindled to narrow streams in a sandy bed.
An inspector asks about cotton and cotton bedding to prevent the spread of pests. They have none of the questioned items, so are allowed to continue.

32.title: The emergency gasoline earns its place
highlights: A stop to chase jackrabbits produces no rabbits and uses up daylight. Miriam watches the sun drop behind the mountains.
Darkness forces them to connect the lights. Shortly afterward the Ford stops: the tank is empty.
Their reserve gasoline gets them the remaining miles into Deming. A free campground is a welcome end to a late and tiring drive.

33.title: At last, the desert they had imagined
highlights: Cooking fuel is so scarce that travelers have split pieces from railway fence posts. Miriam admits her family has taken a share too.
After so many disappointing versions of 'desert,' a long stretch of sand and scant grass finally matches their mental picture.
Century plants become another roadside study. Miriam examines the sharp leaves, exposed roots, and tall old flower stalks.

33.title: An unmarked fork and another state
highlights: Heat and passing cars' dust make the drive uncomfortable. At an unmarked fork, they have to ask other travelers which way to go.
Sharp curves and narrow mountain roads bring them toward Arizona. A brief engine repair interrupts the climb.
They reach Duncan and camp in the foothills. For once, the evening feels warm.

34.title: Flowers among the rocks
highlights: The family watches a road crew drill through rock with compressed-air equipment. New roads promise wider grades and concrete bridges.
High in the mountains they stop to gather yellow daisies and red poppies growing between the rocks.
Bluebirds, butterflies, and hot sunshine make nearby Christmas displays seem strange. The weather hardly feels like late November.

34.title: Grover's rifle and a frightening night stop
highlights: After missing a jackrabbit five times, Grover throws away his rifle in anger. The others cannot help laughing.
Misleading expectations about the next town leave them on a steep grade after dark, out of gas again. They reach for the emergency supply.
A fast car comes around a bend where two vehicles cannot pass. It stops short, but the scare leads to a heated argument before the family finally reaches camp.

35.title: Higher than anything at home
highlights: The children want to climb the mountain outside camp. Once on the road, great cuts, copper workings, and canyon views make earlier hills seem small.
They stop for dinner high above the rest of the world. The next climbs leave them wishing they had not eaten: looking down makes their stomachs turn.
Then a door gives way and Beulah tumbles out. They retrieve her before another car rounds the bend; Miriam knows how much worse it could have been.

35.title: Top of the World, then down into Devil's Canyon
highlights: A mountaintop station is aptly named Top of the World. Beyond it, great balancing boulders and rock walls make the scenery both magnificent and frightening.
They repeatedly stop to tighten the brakes. A wrecked Buick below the road is an unwelcome reminder of the danger.
A tunnel cut through solid rock and the winding descent toward Superior become unforgettable sights. Their rule for the day is Safety First.

35.title: Even the desert feels safer now
highlights: After the mountain pass, the family welcomes the prospect of level desert. They share water with another motorist whose radiator hose has failed.
Heat allows the children to go barefoot, but passing cars raise clouds of dust. Miriam cannot imagine choosing this road for a pleasure drive.
At camp, they agree that all the earlier mountains were mere playthings beside this day's road from Globe toward Superior.

36.title: Oranges on the trees and honey for the road
highlights: Near Mesa, the family sees oranges growing on trees for the first time. Roses, fruit, and beehives make the watered valley especially appealing.
They stop for sweet oranges, apples, and a quart of honey. The new place becomes something they can taste as well as admire.
A long repair stop near Phoenix interrupts the pleasure. This time a pull to restart the Ford is free, and they move on to camp at Cashion.

37.title: Across the spillway instead of the bridge
highlights: A repair on a one-car-wide road brings a line of impatient motorists honking behind them. Miriam refuses to be hurried.
At Gillespie Dam, a washed-out bridge means driving across a broad paved spillway through several inches of flowing water.
Desert flowers still bloom beside the road. After another long drive, the little settlement at Mohawk looks good simply because they are tired and nearly out of daylight.

37.title: A match at the gasoline tank
highlights: While Miriam prepares supper, another motorist lights a match to see how full the gasoline tank is.
Flames catch both the filling hose and luggage wrapped in canvas. The family tries to start its own Ford so it can get away.
The fire is put out before they have to move. Everyone is badly frightened; an otherwise pleasant, warm evening has come close to disaster.

38.title: California begins with an inspection
highlights: They pause to help another man start his car, then cross the Colorado River at Yuma.
Plant inspectors require suitcases, bags, boxes, and the cupboard to be opened. Everything is checked before the family can enter California.
Released at last, they stop for their first California dinner. The celebration is especially welcome because the inspection has delayed the meal.

38.title: A wooden road disappearing under the sand
highlights: High sand drifts finally make California look like the desert the family expected. Even a small breeze begins to sweep sand across the road.
Beside the new route lies an old wooden road, only one car wide except for passing places. Parts are already buried.
They camp near Holtville and hear irrigation water running nearby. The station-keeping couple is sociable: another roadside welcome after a strange landscape.

39.title: A Thanksgiving that feels like the Fourth
highlights: The heat makes Thanksgiving feel more like the Fourth of July. Lunch is prepared during yet another repair, and shade seems a blessing.
The men finally satisfy their curiosity by weighing the rig. The supposedly free answer costs a quarter: 4,900 pounds, without Clarence and Kenneth.
There is no conventional holiday feast in this entry, just the work and small discoveries of another traveling day.

39.title: A remembered joke beside the Salton Sea
highlights: The sea stays in view through much of the afternoon. Signs advertise excellent duck shooting, but the family jokes that another hunting trip might cost Grover another gun.
The joke reaches back to his discarded rifle in Arizona: one day's mishap has become part of the family's shared story.
Desert alternating with fruit groves astonishes Miriam. She thinks the change wrought by water sounds like a fairy tale until seen with one's own eyes.

40.title: A rainbow flashing up the mountainside
highlights: Clouds alternately hide and reveal the peaks. The family enjoys watching the mountains appear and disappear.
A brilliantly colored rainbow seems to rise out of the desert and flash up the mountain. Miriam calls it one of the most beautiful sights they have ever seen.
Wind-bent trees and their first California shower add to the sense of entering a different world.

40.title: Getting ready for the last lap
highlights: Orchards line the road. Large oil-burning pots between the trees reveal how growers protect fruit when frost threatens.
Red rose hedges, laden orange trees, and Riverside's streets make a strong impression after so much empty country.
As the sun drops behind the mountains, they stop at a filling station. Everyone gets a good cleaning, ready for the final day's journey.

41.title: Long Beach at last
highlights: After a night of heavy rain, they set out for the final stretch. Signal Hill's crowded oil wells announce the approach to Long Beach.
The last miles feel painfully slow. At half past twelve they reach their destination, eat, and visit: everyone is happy.
That afternoon they go to see the Pacific. Its roaring breakers astonish Miriam, but both she and Clarence find its immense power unsettling rather than inviting.

41.title: The one chance of a lifetime
highlights: Back with the family, everyone is relieved not to have to think about traveling farther for a while.
Miriam looks back over 2,809 miles, the good country and the poor, and is glad they did not miss their chance to make the journey.
She knows parts of the diary may sound far-fetched. Her closing invitation is to take the trip and see it all for oneself: seeing is believing.
